analysis.one_liner: Cuts the top capital gains tax rate to 14% for individuals and 28% for corporations, and indexes gains for inflation.
analysis.headline: Backed by 45 House members from both parties, the bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cut the maximum tax rate on capital gains to 14% for individuals (down from the 20% set in 1997) and 28% for corporations (down from 35%), and would adjust the purchase price of stocks and property held more than three years upward for inflation, so gains caused only by rising prices would not be taxed. It would also repeal an existing tax break for small-business stock and tighten the rules for deducting capital losses. Because most capital gains are realized by higher-income households, the rate cut would concentrate its benefits at the top while reducing federal revenue.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors who sell appreciated assets, especially the highest-income households who realize the large majority of capital gains, plus corporations selling appreciated property, who would see their rate drop from 35% to 28%. Owners of stock, business property, and real estate held over three years would gain from inflation indexing, and mutual fund investors would inherit those adjustments through their funds.

how_it_helps.text: The maximum capital gains rate for individuals would fall to 14%, down from the 20% rate in effect after the 1997 tax act, and the corporate capital gains rate would fall from 35% to 28%.

Assets held more than three years would get their cost basis indexed to inflation using the GDP deflator, so taxes would apply only to real gains, not gains that merely reflect rising prices; the adjustment flows through mutual funds, REITs, partnerships, and S corporations to their investors.
The 14% rate would also apply under the individual alternative minimum tax, preventing the AMT from clawing back the lower rate.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and ultimately other taxpayers, through the revenue lost from lower rates and indexing. Repeal of the small-business stock exclusion and the new limits on deducting capital losses would offset some of that cost, and taxpayers who lose money on investments would lose the ability to deduct up to $3,000 of net capital losses against ordinary income.

drawbacks.text: The rate cuts would primarily benefit households at the top of the income distribution, who realize most capital gains, while the lost revenue would have to be made up through other taxes, reduced spending, or borrowing.

The bill repeals the section 1202 exclusion for gain on small-business stock, removing an existing targeted break for small-company investors, and it bars individuals from deducting net capital losses against ordinary income, which hurts investors whose investments lose money.
Inflation indexing by asset and holding period would add significant recordkeeping and compliance complexity for taxpayers, funds, and the IRS.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a good-faith case for the indexing provision: taxing gains that only reflect inflation taxes money the owner never really earned, and indexing fixes that for long-held property, which includes middle-class homes and small business assets. But the bill's dominant feature is the deep rate cut, whose benefits flow overwhelmingly to the households and corporations that own appreciated assets, at a substantial cost to federal revenue. The small-business exclusion repeal and loss-deduction limits partly claw back the benefit for smaller investors. On balance, the design serves asset holders far more than it serves the broad public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative David Dreier introduced the bill on January 6, 1999, the first day of the 106th Congress, joined by six original cosponsors including both Republicans and Democrats.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction.
Forty-five members cosponsored the bill: 39 Republicans and 6 Democrats.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — was ever recorded before the Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without any action, the federal Treasury kept the revenue that the rate cut and indexing would have cost, and the existing 20% capital gains rate and small-business stock exclusion remained in place. Wealthy asset holders, the bill's main intended beneficiaries, gained nothing beyond the rates they already had.

for.name: Rep. David Dreier
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 6, 1999, the opening day of the 106th Congress.

for.name: 6 of 211 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Ms. McCarthy of Missouri, Mr. Deutsch, and Mr. Moran of Virginia.

against.name: Rep. Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or committee vote; the bill saw no action after referral.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — 39 of 45 cosponsors were Republicans and 6 were Democrats — but no votes were ever recorded, so the actual partisan split on the bill is unknown.

industries.industry: Securities investors and investment management (mutual funds, brokerages)
industries.note: A 14% rate plus inflation indexing would let investors keep a larger share of gains, with the largest dollar benefits flowing to the wealthiest households who own most appreciated stock. Fund investors would inherit the indexing through their funds, but the Treasury would lose the offsetting revenue.
Corporate capital gains would be taxed at 28% instead of the 35% regular rate, a direct tax cut on asset sales. Corporations benefit, while other taxpayers bear the lost revenue.
Tangible property and REIT shares held more than three years would qualify for inflation indexing, reducing tax on property sales. Real (non-inflation) gains would still be taxed.

Sellers of long-held business assets would gain from the lower rate and indexing, but the bill repeals the existing 50% exclusion for gain on qualified small-business stock, removing a break some small-company investors currently use.
